items.stimulus:
Mangroves are trees and shrubs that grow in the salty, oxygen-poor mud of tropical and subtropical shorelines, where few other woody plants can survive. Some species prop themselves up on arching stilt roots; others send pencil-like breathing roots up through the mud. Together these tangled structures form a dense, porous barrier, and over recent decades coastal engineers have taken a growing interest in what that barrier does to the sea.

When a wave enters a mangrove stand, much of its energy is spent pushing water past thousands of roots and trunks. Field measurements have repeatedly shown that wave height falls as a wave travels inland through the forest, and that the reduction is greatest where the trees are densest and the belt is widest. Even a fairly narrow belt can noticeably reduce ordinary wind-driven waves. Storm surges, which raise the level of the whole sea for hours, are a different matter: belts measured in kilometres rather than metres are needed to make a substantial difference, and even then the effect is partial. The roots also slow the water enough for suspended sediment to settle, so a healthy forest can gradually build up the ground beneath it.

None of this makes mangroves a substitute for every sea wall. Their protective value depends on the width, density and health of the stand, and on the type of hazard. Yet they offer advantages that concrete cannot: they recover by themselves after moderate damage, they shelter young fish on which local fisheries depend, and their waterlogged soils lock away large amounts of carbon.

Despite this, large areas of mangrove have been cleared during the last half-century, much of it for fish and shrimp ponds, timber and coastal building. Restoration projects have had mixed results. Seedlings planted on mudflats where mangroves never naturally grew often die, whereas efforts that first restore the natural flow of tides to former mangrove sites tend to succeed more often. Many researchers conclude that the forest is best treated as one part of a coastal defence system, planned alongside engineered structures rather than in competition with them.

items.stimulus:
Freedom-of-information laws give members of the public a legal right to request documents held by government bodies. Sweden is usually credited with the earliest such law, passed in 1766 as part of a statute on press freedom, but most countries adopted comparable legislation only in the second half of the twentieth century or later. The United States passed its federal act in 1966, and Australia's federal act followed in 1982.

Although the details differ, most of these laws share a common design. A person need not explain why they want a document; the starting presumption is that official information should be released unless a specific exemption applies. Typical exemptions protect national security, personal privacy, commercial secrets supplied by private firms and the confidential deliberations of senior ministers. An agency that refuses a request must usually give reasons, and the applicant can ask for the decision to be reviewed, often by an independent commissioner or tribunal.

Supporters argue that the mere possibility of disclosure encourages officials to keep careful records and to act as if their decisions might one day be examined in public. Critics within government reply that the same possibility can have the opposite effect: advice may be given orally, or written in vague terms, so that nothing embarrassing is ever on file. Both effects are hard to measure, because the evidence for each consists largely of documents that were, or were not, created.

In practice, the value of these laws depends heavily on how they are administered. Long delays, high processing charges and broad readings of the exemptions can leave a generous statute with little force, while a modest statute applied in good faith may achieve a great deal.

items.stimulus:
Many people now accept that the way we treat at least some animals is a moral matter, but they disagree about which animals count and why. One influential answer is that what matters is sentience: the capacity to have experiences that feel good or bad to the one having them. On this view, a creature deserves moral consideration not because of its cleverness or its likeness to humans, but because its life can go better or worse from its own point of view. A river that is dammed is changed, yet there is nothing it is like for the river to lose its course; a hen kept where she cannot spread her wings is in a different position altogether.

The appeal of the criterion is that it seems to pick out the very feature that makes harm possible. Intelligence, by contrast, looks like the wrong kind of property: a quick-witted animal and a slow one may both be in distress when injured, and it is unclear why the distress of the quicker one should weigh more.

The difficulty lies in applying the criterion. Experience is private, so sentience in other creatures must be inferred from indirect signs, such as the structure of the nervous system, behaviour that guards an injured part of the body, or a willingness to accept a cost in order to avoid a harmful stimulus. For mammals and birds such signs are plentiful. For fish, octopuses and crabs the evidence has grown considerably in recent decades, and several jurisdictions have extended some legal protections to such animals as a result. For insects the picture remains much less certain.

Some ethicists respond that, where the evidence is uncertain but not negligible, the sensible course is to give the animal the benefit of the doubt, especially when protecting it costs little. Others warn that extending concern too widely could dilute protections for animals whose capacity to feel is well established. Even so, both camps tend to agree that the question to ask is whether an animal can feel, not how closely it resembles us.

For most of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, a lighthouse needed people. The lamp, burning oil and later kerosene, had to be lit at dusk, its wick trimmed through the night so that it did not smoke, and its fuel topped up. In many towers the great lens turned on a clockwork mechanism driven by a falling weight, which a keeper had to wind back up every few hours. Keepers also cleaned soot and salt from the glass, recorded the weather in a logbook and, at stations with fog signals, sounded those signals whenever visibility fell.

The work was demanding less because of any single task than because it never stopped. At remote rock stations, where there was no room for families, keepers usually worked in small teams and rotated between weeks on the light and periods ashore. At mainland stations, by contrast, keepers often lived on site with their families, and some children grew up knowing no other home.

Automation arrived gradually. Electric lamps that could be switched on by light-sensitive devices removed the need to tend a flame; electric motors replaced clockwork; and radio and later telephone links allowed a single depot to monitor many lights at once. Each change reduced the number of keepers a station required, long before the last of them were withdrawn. In Britain the final staffed lighthouse was automated in 1998.

Lighthouse authorities justified automation chiefly on grounds of cost, although they also pointed out that well-designed equipment did not tire or fall ill. Former keepers sometimes replied that a person on site could notice things a machine could not, such as a small vessel in difficulty close to the rocks. items.stimulus:
Graphite, the soft grey material in pencil cores, is made of stacked sheets of carbon atoms, each sheet a flat mesh of hexagons. For decades physicists discussed what a single such sheet might be like, and some doubted that one could exist on its own without crumpling or curling up. In 2004 two researchers at the University of Manchester, Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov, showed that it could. Their method was strikingly low-tech: they used ordinary adhesive tape to peel thinner and thinner flakes from a piece of graphite until some flakes were only one atom thick, then located these on a specially prepared silicon wafer under an optical microscope. The material, named graphene, earned the pair the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2010.

Graphene's properties attracted attention at once. Weight for weight, it is among the strongest materials ever tested. It conducts electricity exceptionally well, with electrons moving through it at high speed and with little scattering, and it conducts heat better than copper. Although it is a continuous sheet of atoms, it absorbs only a small fraction of the light that falls on it, so a single layer is almost transparent. It is also impermeable to most gases.

Turning these properties into products has proved harder than early enthusiasm suggested. Making large, flawless sheets cheaply remains difficult, and the tape method, ideal for laboratory study, is useless for industrial production. Another obstacle concerns electronics. Silicon chips depend on materials that can be switched sharply between conducting and non-conducting states, and pure graphene, unlike silicon, lacks the property that allows such clean switching. Researchers have tried to engineer that property into graphene, but usually at the cost of some of its other advantages.

Graphene has nonetheless found uses where its strengths matter and its weaknesses do not, for example as an additive in composite materials, coatings and some batteries. Its isolation also prompted a search for other materials only one or a few atoms thick, a field that has since grown well beyond carbon.

When large numbers of office employees began working from home, public discussion focused at first on productivity: whether people would do as much work without a manager nearby. Less attention was paid to what the office had been quietly supplying all along, namely a steady stream of casual social contact. Brief conversations in a corridor or at a kitchen bench rarely appear in a job description, yet for many people they are a significant part of the day's social life, and for some, particularly those who live alone or have recently moved to a new city, they may be the main part.

Researchers who study loneliness distinguish between social isolation, which is an objective shortage of contact with others, and loneliness, which is the subjective feeling that one's connections are inadequate. The two do not always coincide. A person can see few people and feel content, or be surrounded by colleagues and feel lonely. Before the middle of the twentieth century, loading a cargo ship was slow, costly work. Goods arrived at the docks in sacks, barrels, crates and bales of every size, and gangs of dockworkers moved them piece by piece into the hold, where they had to be packed tightly so that nothing shifted at sea. A ship might spend as long in port being loaded and unloaded as it did crossing the ocean, and theft and breakage along the way were routine.

Within roughly fifteen years, international agreement on standard container sizes allowed the same box to travel by ship, train and truck across national borders, and specialised cranes and vessels were built around it.

The number of dockworkers needed to move a given quantity of cargo fell sharply, which led to prolonged disputes in many ports.

items.stimulus:
Silent films were rarely watched in silence. From the early years of cinema, screenings were accompanied by live music, and by the 1920s the range of accompaniment was enormous. A small-town hall might employ a single pianist, while the grandest city cinemas kept full orchestras and installed elaborate theatre organs capable of imitating drums, bells, birdsong and train whistles.

What the musicians played varied as widely as who played it. Some accompanists improvised throughout, watching the screen and adjusting mood and tempo as the action changed. Others drew on large published collections of short pieces sorted by emotional character, such as tension, pursuit, grief or comedy, which could be strung together to suit a given film. To help, film distributors often issued cue sheets: lists of suggested pieces with notes indicating where each should begin. For a small number of prestigious productions, composers wrote complete original scores, which were sent to cinemas large enough to perform them.

The quality of the result depended heavily on the individual musician. A skilled accompanist could heighten suspense or rescue an awkward scene, and audiences in some towns followed favourite performers much as they followed favourite actors. A careless one might play a cheerful tune during a funeral, and trade papers of the period printed complaints about exactly such lapses.

The arrival of synchronised sound in the late 1920s brought this world to a rapid end. Once music could be recorded onto the film itself, cinemas no longer needed to employ musicians, and within a few years many thousands of players had lost their jobs. Musicians' organisations campaigned against the change, without lasting success. In recent decades, however, live accompaniment has returned in a different form: restored silent films are now often screened at festivals and in concert halls with new or reconstructed scores performed live, giving audiences a chance to experience the films roughly as they were first presented.

For a long time sleep was regarded mainly as a period of rest during which the brain was largely idle. Research over recent decades has replaced this picture with a far more active one, in which sleep helps to turn the experiences of the day into lasting memories.

Much of the evidence concerns a structure called the hippocampus, which is heavily involved in forming new memories of events and places. In experiments with rats, researchers recorded the activity of hippocampal cells that fire when an animal is at particular spots in a maze. During later sleep, the same cells sometimes fired again in the same order as during the run, but compressed into a much shorter time, as though the route were being rehearsed. Such replay occurs especially during deep, slow-wave sleep, and is thought to help transfer information to the cortex, the brain's outer layer, where memories can be stored for the longer term.

Studies in people point in a similar direction. Volunteers who learn a list of word pairs and then sleep generally recall more of the list the next day than volunteers who spend the same interval awake. The benefit appears larger for some kinds of material than for others, and different stages of sleep may favour different kinds of memory; the stage associated with vivid dreaming, for example, has been linked in some studies to emotional memories, although those findings are less consistent.

Sleep also matters before learning. People deprived of a night's sleep tend to form new memories less effectively the following day, which suggests that sleep restores the brain's capacity to take in information as well as consolidating what has already been learned.

Researchers caution that consolidation is not simple copying. Memories appear to be reorganised during sleep: some details fade while general patterns are strengthened, which may help explain why people sometimes wake with a clearer grasp of a problem than they had the night before.

items.stimulus:
The first machine translation systems, developed from the 1950s onwards, relied on rules written by linguists: dictionaries that paired words in two languages and grammars that described how sentences should be rearranged. Such systems worked tolerably on narrow, carefully written texts but stumbled over the irregularity of ordinary language. From around 1990, researchers shifted towards statistical methods, which learned likely correspondences between phrases by analysing large collections of texts that had already been translated by people. Since the mid-2010s, most systems have used neural networks that process whole sentences at once, and the fluency of their output has improved markedly.

This history explains much about what current systems do well and badly. Because they learn from existing translations, they perform best between languages for which vast amounts of such material exist, and in subject areas, such as news or technical manuals, that are well represented in it. For languages with few digitised translations, quality is usually much lower.

Even for well-resourced languages, some problems persist. A system must often choose between meanings that the source sentence leaves open. A word may have several senses that only the wider context distinguishes; one language may mark whether a speaker is being formal or familiar, or the gender of a person, where another leaves this unstated, forcing the system to guess. Because most systems translate one sentence at a time or consider only a limited stretch of surrounding text, such guesses may be inconsistent across a long document.

A further difficulty arises from the very fluency that makes modern output attractive. Older systems produced visibly awkward sentences, which warned readers to be cautious. Neural systems tend to produce smooth, natural-sounding text even when the meaning is wrong, and occasionally add or omit content altogether. An error is therefore harder to notice, particularly for a reader who does not know the source language and so cannot check.

For these reasons, professional translators increasingly use machine output as a first draft to be revised rather than as a finished product, and in fields where mistakes carry serious consequences, such as medicine and law, careful human review remains essential.

Since the mid-2010s, most systems have used neural networks that process whole sentences at once, and the fluency of their output has improved markedly.

This history explains much about what current systems do well and badly. Because they learn from existing translations, they perform best between languages for which vast amounts of such material exist, and in subject areas, such as news or technical manuals, that are well represented in it. For languages with few digitised translations, quality is usually much lower.

Even for well-resourced languages, some problems persist. A system must often choose between meanings that the source sentence leaves open. A word may have several senses that only the wider context distinguishes; one language may mark whether a speaker is being formal or familiar, or the gender of a person, where another leaves this unstated, forcing the system to guess. Because most systems translate one sentence at a time or consider only a limited stretch of surrounding text, such guesses may be inconsistent across a long document.

A further difficulty arises from the very fluency that makes modern output attractive. Older systems produced visibly awkward sentences, which warned readers to be cautious. Neural systems tend to produce smooth, natural-sounding text even when the meaning is wrong, and occasionally add or omit content altogether. An error is therefore harder to notice, particularly for a reader who does not know the source language and so cannot check.

For these reasons, professional translators increasingly use machine output as a first draft to be revised rather than as a finished product, and in fields where mistakes carry serious consequences, such as medicine and law, careful human review remains essential.

items.explanation_ko: 1) 코디네이터는 대체 튜터를 구하는 데 며칠이 필요한데, 당일 오후에야 알리면(on Thursday afternoon) 대체를 구할 수 없어 아이들과 다른 튜터에게 부담을 준다. 2) 늦게라도 알리기는 하고 다른 정규 튜터가 있으므로 수업이 완전히 무너지지는 않는다. 3) 약속을 늦게 알리는 것은 해서는 안 되므로 B가 아니고, 아무 연락 없이 빠지는 것보다는 피해가 작으므로 D도 아니다. → 정답 C (부적절하지만 심각하지 않음)
